title: Measurement-versus-model parity plot
summary: Every model prediction is plotted against its measurement, with a 1:1 line, a percentage band and error metrics. Points on the line are perfect agreement; the scatter around it is the error.

media.alt: Scatter of model prediction against measured temperature with a 1:1 dashed line, a shaded plus or minus ten percent band, horizontal error bars and a box of error metrics.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How well does the model reproduce the measurement?
read_the_figure.axes: x: measured value in K. y: model prediction in K, same range and same scale (square aspect), 250 to 1900 K. Dashed amber: 1:1 line. Shaded band: plus and minus 10 percent. Error bars: measurement uncertainty on x. Text: RMSE 43 K, MAPE 3.4 percent, R^2 = 0.989, n = 70.
look_at: Are points evenly scattered on both sides of the 1:1 line?
Is the scatter growing with the value (a funnel)?
How many points are outside the 10 percent band?
Do the horizontal error bars explain the scatter?
read_the_figure.proves: Points on the 1:1 line within the band show that the model reproduces the measurements on this set. Metrics summarise it. It does not show the model holds outside the measured range.
if_wrong: Unequal axes or no 1:1 line: the reader cannot judge agreement.
A trend away from the line at one end: a systematic bias.
Only R^2 quoted: a high R^2 is easy to get over a wide range.

terms.meaning: Scatter of predictions against observations with the 1:1 line.
Root mean square error, in the units of the data.
One minus the ratio of the residual to the total sum of squares.
Mean of (model minus measurement); a systematic shift.

remember: RMSE = sqrt(mean((p - m)^2)), units of the data.
MAPE = mean(|p - m| / m) x 100 percent.
Square axes with the 1:1 line; show a band.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along x is the measurement, along y the prediction, with equal axes so the 1:1 line is at 45 degrees. Teal dots with horizontal bars are data with measurement uncertainty, the amber dashed line is perfect agreement, a shaded amber band shows plus or minus 10 percent, and the text box gives three metrics.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Agreement between two numbers is a distance from the diagonal, which the eye measures well. A parity plot collapses everything else (time, position, condition) and leaves only the question that matters here: how close is the model to the measurement. Metrics beside the plot give the numbers, the band says what is acceptable.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Is the scatter evenly distributed? Points lie on both sides of the dashed line over the whole range; the scatter grows from about 15 K at 400 K to 70 K at 1700 K, a funnel in absolute terms. Q2: How many points are outside the band? None clearly lie outside the shaded plus or minus 10 percent wedge, in agreement with MAPE = 3.4 percent. Q3: Is R^2 = 0.989 good news? Check it: the measurements spread over about 300 to 1800 K, so s_m is about 430 K; 1 - (43/433)^2 = 0.990. It comes mainly from the wide range, so the RMSE of 43 K is the better figure.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: 1:1 line and error metric: the line is the reference for agreement and the metric is the number the reader can compare with other models. Missing either, the plot is a cloud.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: R^2 rewards a wide range: with the measurements spanning 300 to 1800 K (standard deviation about 430 K) an RMSE of 43 K gives R^2 = 0.99, which sounds perfect but is a 10 percent of the spread. A single average hides a bias with the value. Error bars on x only treat the model as exact. Points drawn on top of each other hide density, and the percentage band widens on a linear axis so it looks more tolerant at high values.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A residual plot against measurement shows structure better; a Bland-Altman plot (difference against mean); a QQ plot of residuals; a table of RMSE by condition.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a residual panel below, error bars on both axes, and RMSE for the lower and upper halves of the range.

steps.title: R squared from RMSE and spread
steps.note: So the same RMSE gives a higher R^2 on a wider range of data.

worked.title: The three metrics on five points
worked.problem: Measured 500, 800, 1100, 1400, 1700 K; predicted 520, 780, 1130, 1380, 1750 K. Compute RMSE, MAPE and R^2.

solution.text: R squared with the mean 1100 K and the sum of squares 1 000 000.

worked.answer: RMSE 30 K, MAPE 2.7 percent, R^2 = 0.995: a high R^2 with errors of 20 to 50 K.

analyze.q: Where would you look for a bias that the three numbers do not show?
The error bars are on x only. What does that assume?

evaluate.q: Is R^2 = 0.99 a good reason to accept the model?
evaluate.hint: What is the spread of the data?

create: Add a residual panel and the RMSE of each half of the range.
Colour the points by pressure or condition and look for clusters.

checks.q: R^2 = 0.99 but the points lie systematically below the line at high values. What do you report?
checks.answer: Report the bias and the RMSE of the upper range: R^2 hides a systematic under-prediction where it may matter most.
